items.a10-h: The Pamir Mountains Disaster – the Worst in the History of Mountaineering
items.a10-p054: The work and contribution of the Israeli team in the attempt to locate the missing*
items.a10-p002: On 13 July 1990 the greatest disaster in the history of mountaineering took place. Some fifty climbers who had gathered for an international event lost their lives in it, among them four Israelis: Benny Agur, Dov Meli, Gabi Manobla and Yuki Pereg, of blessed memory, members of the Israeli Alpine Club. The disaster happened at night, the result of an earthquake that made great blocks of ice, "seracs", collapse, and sent avalanches of snow onto the tents pitched in a small valley known as "the Frying Pan", at an altitude of 3,005 metres, where the climbers were camped on their way to Lenin Peak (7,200 m) in the Pamir range. This range is the highest of the ranges of the former Soviet Union, and it forms the border between the Islamic republics of Tajikistan to the south and Kyrgyzstan to the north. The search lasted 26 days, until the authorities decided that it had been exhausted.
items.a10-src1: *Part of this article was published in "Masa Acher" on 15 September 2008 (with thanks to Moshe Gilad).
items.a10-p003: Prof. Agursky, Benny Agur's father and a Sovietologist with connections in Israel and in the Soviet Union, noticed a low-key report of the disaster in the Soviet press. Together with the other families he started a vigorous fund-raising campaign to finance a rescue expedition, and turned to the "Israeli Alpine Club"† (see the article "Return to the Place You Came From") to work towards setting it up. Of the Foreign Ministry he demanded, and indeed obtained, action at the political level so that the expedition could reach the disaster area. Despite the multinational nature of the tragic event, the Israeli search and rescue team was the only foreign team that came forward to help, and its contribution won great appreciation in the media and among the public of what was then the Soviet Union.
items.a10-p004: From high up on the crane in the date plantation at Ein Gedi, in 42 degrees in the shade, I saw two men running towards me and signalling to me to come down. They introduced themselves as people from the Foreign Ministry, told me about the disaster in the Pamirs, and said that since I was an officer for locating missing persons, with experience and qualifications on ice and snow, they were asking me to go out there at once; they would take care of all the arrangements. I made it clear to them that this was not a task for one person but for a skilled team, equipped with clothing and gear that could hardly be obtained in Israel. But the main thing was that eight years had passed since I had retired from snow-and-ice mountaineering, with a firm decision not to go back to it; what is more, <span epub:type="pagebreak" role="doc-pagebreak" id="pg-67" title="63"/>the date harvest was upon us – the most pressing and important season of the date branch – and I did not even have a valid passport. And I don't speak Russian either, I added.
items.a10-p005: I was sure that would be the end of it, but they were set on their goal, and asked me to prepare a list of equipment by six in the evening and to stay available by phone. In the evening they rang and said that the next day a car would come to take me to choose equipment from the store of an elite unit, which held everything needed for operations from the ocean floor to the summits of the Himalayas. As far as the kibbutz and the dates were concerned, everything had already been approved, and two Russian-speaking alpinists, members of the club, would join me later: I would meet Bella at Ben Gurion Airport, and Dima was at that moment on a course in Chamonix (Mont Blanc); he was already acclimatized to altitude and would join us in Zurich. I had run out of excuses, but not out of fears.
items.a10-p006: Just before take-off they brought me a new passport, and someone put a large, heavy video camera in my lap, without grasping the physiological meaning of the swift passage from the vineyards of Ein Gedi to the glaciers of the Pamirs. I decided that I would throw the camera into the first crevasse I met, without the slightest pang of conscience.
items.a10-p007: From our embassy in Moscow we gathered that dollar bribes and "Marlboro" cigarettes were the oil that would move the various and curious means of transport we would need to reach the foot of the Pamir range, and this was borne out in full later on. We had to get to Dushanbe, the capital of Tajikistan, but at the airport for domestic flights they would not let us through without an outrageous handout of "greenbacks". In Dushanbe we had enough time for a first acquaintance with the typical faces of the people of Central Asia. The varied, fresh abundance in the markets was astonishing, compared with the shameful poverty of what Moscow had to offer.
items.a10-p008: The onward flight was to the small town of Jirgatal – the last airstrip before the Pamir range – in a small plane. Every seat and aisle was crammed with men and women with packs of produce, and with a few goats they had not managed to sell in Dushanbe. I went straight to the impassive pilot and waved our tickets, but he ignored me. When I pulled out two packs of Marlboro he showed interest and demanded a third. Then, with the help of the co-pilot, he compressed the contents of the plane, the human contents included, and cleared three seats amid shouts and bleats of protest.
items.a10-p009: The last leg of the flight was in a passenger helicopter that crossed exceptionally high ranges. The view was wonderful, and below the snow line herds could be seen grazing on green slopes. Here and there smoke rose from a Kyrgyz yurt (temporary summer housing). Whenever one of the passengers suffered from lack of oxygen, the flight engineer would press a mask connected to an oxygen cylinder to that passenger's face.
items.a10-p010: I had not known our missing climbers, and when we reached the base camp at Achik Tash (3,600 m), Boris led us to their tent. Through video cassettes of their preparations in the Caucasus, which fitted the camera we had brought, I gained some idea of what they looked like, of their personalities and of the social dynamics among them. (Link to the video – at the end of the article)
items.a10-p012: Boris, a Jewish intellectual and a member of the Leningrad Alpine Club, had visited Israel shortly before the disaster and brought the Israeli club the news of the coming Pamir event. Benny, Dov, Gadi and Yuki, of blessed memory, got "fired up" and decided to take part. The experienced Boris took them under his wing, including days of training and acclimatization in the High Caucasus. After the tents had been pitched in the valley of the Frying Pan, he went down to the lower camp for some purpose, and when he came back to the Frying Pan in the morning,
items.a10-p013: he was stunned to find it empty of tents and people. Boris is the tragic hero of the event, in which he lost 23 of his fellow club members, his partner among them, as well as the Israelis who had been under his wing. He was also the almost exclusive source of reliable information about the disaster, which he passed on to me in a detailed debriefing during the domestic flights from Moscow to the
items.a10-p016: Our main task for the next day was acclimatization to the thin air. We knew that the quickest and most effective way to achieve it was to climb to the next camp (4,400 m) and come back down, and so we agreed to do. With difficulty and much suffering we reached the next camp and collapsed on the ground, exhausted, gripped by nausea and headaches. My colleagues did not keep to what we had agreed and refused to go down "only to come up again tomorrow". They knew very well that this was what had to be done, but they could not take it in. I forced myself to go down, hoping they would follow me, but they held to their refusal. So I went down alone, and the next day climbed up again, this time with relative ease. I found my colleagues still in the grip of altitude sickness and decided to go on to the site of the disaster, to get acquainted with the searchers and join them. After another twenty-four hours my colleagues recovered and joined as well.
items.a10-p017: I wanted to coordinate our work, so as not to repeat what had been done before us, but we found no figure of a leader there. Everyone did their best, but without an orderly plan. Moreover, there was a constant turnover of volunteers, with no information, records or documentation passing between them. We learned that on the first day of the search two injured survivors and three bodies had been found, and that the rest still counted as missing; someone also told me that a shoe with Hebrew letters had been found, but the finder was no longer there, and nobody knew where the shoe was, or where and when it had been found. Naturally I was disappointed by the absence of the basic rules of locating missing persons, and I said so gently and hesitantly. My remarks were received willingly and even with appreciation, and I was promised that from then on they would be followed.
items.a10-p018: The first camp became a secondary logistics base: a helicopter brought equipment and volunteers up there from the base camp, as well as two large cartons we had brought from Israel. The camp was run by Yuri, a retired alpinist, who relayed messages by radio between the base camp and the Frying Pan. A large tent served there as dining room and kitchen, where several of the partners of the missing laboured to keep mould and rot away from the ingredients meant for the evening meals of the volunteers coming down from the Frying Pan.
items.a10-p019: The contents of our cartons were mostly surprising emergency food from the stores of the unit mentioned above: chiefly powders in thin packets which, with water added and a brief boil, swell into tasty, nourishing and filling mashed potato and soups, and also a large quantity of small, dry salami sausages. To these the families in Israel had added quantities of chocolate and treats of every kind, as well as Ultrasol and protective lip balms of high quality compared with what the volunteers had improvised.
items.a10-p020: One day we announced that this time we would make the meal. We came down from the Frying Pan a little early, lowered the rolled-up sides of the tent, prepared a feast fit for a king, and when the volunteers arrived we revealed the laid tables. The amazement was great. One of the women said she was no longer surprised by the Israelis – we were riding the ripples of the waves of worldwide admiration that the Home Front Command delegation had justly earned for its work in an earthquake disaster in Turkey some time before – and after peeking into the rubbish bins she added: "All the same, it's amazing where all the peelings have gone."
items.a10-p021: As "head of the Israeli team" I was asked to a coordination meeting at the base camp with the "heads of the rescue teams" of the Islamic republics that share the mountain between them. I was surprised: I knew nothing about them and had not seen them on the mountain. Down below it turned out that they were a kind of clerks, busy with lists of equipment and volunteers. I found them around a bottle of drink with their radio operators, the Kyrgyz one (who is Russian) sipping from a cup in one hand while his radio operator filled the cup in his other hand. According to Boris, the bottle was kept full thanks to the radio operator, who pilfered alcohol from the first-aid kits in the tents of the alpinists who had gone up the mountain.
items.a10-p022: The Tajik's radio operator, also a Russian (hereafter Sergei), knew a little English, and explained to me that I had been invited because an important newspaper correspondent had arrived "to cover the search". When the interview was over, I took the radio operator aside so that he could explain why the helicopter flew only to the first camp and did not reach the Frying Pan. His answer was that the air there was too thin to allow it. I thanked him, strengthened the new friendship with a pack of Marlboro, and hurried to the helicopter that was taking volunteers back to Jirgatal, for a briefing with Prof. Agursky. The professor was a genius at human relations no less than he was a Sovietologist, and there he had been given generous hospitality in the home of a local family, and a communications service with Israel and the world through a radio amateur. I went back to Sergei with the news that the helicopter data I had passed on to Israel allowed a landing at the Frying Pan, and handed him three bags holding a pack of Marlboro, salami and "Egozi" chocolate bars, for him and for the helicopter crew. The bags served their purpose until the work on the mountain was over!
items.a10-p023: I understood nothing of the interview. Back in Israel I had the privilege of reading its Hebrew translation, made by my father-in-law, a former cultural attaché at the embassy in Moscow, who went on following the Soviet press. The content of the interview was utterly absurd, but the coincidence was interesting.
items.a10-p024: The landing of the helicopter at the Frying Pan made the moving of volunteers and equipment much easier, and it is a great pity that it had not occurred to me to act on the matter sooner. Towards the last week of the search we received valuable reinforcements: four more members of our club, Shai, Alon, Danny <span epub:type="pagebreak" role="doc-pagebreak" id="pg-72" title="68"/>and Doron. August was approaching, a month prone to avalanches; above all, I feared the moment when the support of the local establishment would stop. With my colleagues' agreement, I decided that we would stay the nights at the Frying Pan and so gain daylight hours for work. We did not allow ourselves to sleep on the comfortable floor of the valley for fear of the "seracs" (the blocks of ice), although sleeping on the slopes was very uncomfortable, to put it mildly.
items.a10-p025: Groups of climbers kept arriving, some of them from countries that had lost people in the disaster; none agreed to help us with the work, apart from an American expedition whose members agreed to stay on for a few hours. Nor did any expedition give up sleeping on the comfortable floor of the Frying Pan, despite our warnings. On sunny days, and most of them were, the heat in the Frying Pan would rise sharply because of the radiation reflected from the snow and from the glaciers around it – hence its name.
items.a10-p026: The Frying Pan site was searched thoroughly by various means, and trenches were cut in the snow and the ice, but nothing was found. This small valley slopes down to a steep glacier split by many deep crevasses. Near its edge a number of objects and items of clothing came to light, and lower down, among the crevasses, more objects were found. It seems, then, that the camp was not buried by the avalanche where it stood, but swept onto the steep glacier, and its occupants, with most of their equipment, were carried into the deep crevasses.
items.a10-p027: Nobody knew how deep the crevasses were. "Those in the know" claimed that some of them surely reached a depth of 50–100 metres, perhaps more. Examining these crevasses meant mortal danger. The blocks of ice around them were unstable, and at their mouths, hanging over nothing, were icicles as sharp as bayonets, which threatened to fall on anyone going down inside and to pierce helmet and wearer alike. I had to use my authority to forbid my colleagues to go near them. Even if the icicles did not break off by themselves, the safety rope, which would inevitably trail behind anyone who dared to go down, could bring them down.
items.a10-p028: Nevertheless, a few of the bravest and most skilful of the Russian alpinists went down to check some of the crevasses. They peered in and hurried to withdraw. After crossing themselves and thanking God that they had come out safely – all of them, of course, confirmed atheists – they reported that examining the crevasses, besides being extremely dangerous, could not be carried through in any case, because blocks of snow and ice from the avalanche, and snow that had fallen since, had formed partial plugs that blocked the way down and hid the bottom.
items.a10-p029: A few volunteers stayed with us at the Frying Pan at night as well, and together we huddled by one of our tents, which became the social and culinary centre, until the plunging temperatures drove us into our sleeping bags. The failure to locate the missing by the usual means made room for irrational conduct, such as a "lucky cockerel" that brought no benefit and ended up in the cooking pot, a dog that stopped working after a short time because of the glare, and a parapsychologist (see "A Friend from Another World" in this book) who believed that powers granted to him from beyond the Earth protected him from altitude sickness and made acclimatization unnecessary.
items.a10-p030: As mentioned, the search for survivors went on for 26 days, until further logistical support was taken from us – chiefly the helicopter, which had been at our disposal almost exclusively. Many dozens of highly experienced Russian alpinists took part in it, most of them from the Leningrad club (Leningrad has since returned to its original name, Saint Petersburg), and we, seven Israelis, in an expedition on behalf of the families and the Israeli Alpine Club.
items.a10-p031: Recognising that there was no chance of reaching the missing, although we knew with high probability where they were, was hard. No wonder, then, that it was hard to tear ourselves away from the mountain and from those buried in it, and the last days of the search were driven by emotion rather than by reason.
items.a10-p033: Statistics show that the Pamir range claims victims every year among the climbers on its slopes. It is true that experience, skill and judgement increase the chances of survival, but blind avalanches like this one, which do not distinguish between a novice and a grand master, are not rare. The more experienced alpinists are, the better they know that in the end their survival is a matter of probability.
items.a10-p034: Two questions recur after every disaster. One is specific: could it have been prevented? The other is more general: why do people take risks when there is no existential need? In conquering glaciers and snowy summits, as in other activities with an adventurous motive, the two questions are bound up with each other, and their root lies in human nature. Risk means a chance of disaster, and the essence of adventure is facing that chance. The next question, therefore – whether the risks of adventure can be reduced – does not seem relevant, since a survival instinct is innate in every person, and adventurers are not suicidal. Since the forces of nature cannot be restrained, it may be better to encourage the climbers' survival instinct through information and education. If this succeeds, the survival instinct will work to persuade its owner to prepare as well as possible for the unequal contest with the forces of nature, which can spring surprises on anyone who bursts onto their home ground.
items.a10-p035: Veterans of adventure, who became aware of the survival instinct in the course of their adventures, naturally strive to refine their capacity for survival through training, proper equipment, curbing recklessness and greater judgement. Others go further and give up from the outset situations in which they might find themselves getting the worst of it against the forces of nature. They turn, for example, to rock climbing below the snow line. Those more exposed to risk are the "unaware", that is, the inexperienced, whose survival instinct has not yet had to raise an outcry. More exposed still are the "unwilling to know", the "it'll be fine" people. Some of them have in the past lost their lives on glaciers, wearing sandals and dressed in shorts. These can sometimes be met at an earlier stage, abseiling in the canyons of the Judaean Desert, in a calm and unhostile setting, joyful and glad of heart at having saved the tuition fees. Most of them stay joyful and glad of heart at least until the next gamble.
items.a10-p036: There is also a minority who, out of self-deception, obey the instinct for adventure as though fulfilling a religious commandment. Its members may quote "Arise, walk through the land" and never omit the "Traveller's Prayer", but they fail at "Take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves", and they belittle, or are unaware of, means of navigation and the amount of water needed.
items.a10-p037: Veterans of adventure, as I said, become aware of the survival instinct, and they must decide whether to refine their capacity for survival ahead of the next adventure or to avoid it. A fierce snowstorm I was caught in in 1982, somewhere in the French Alps, made me decide to give up those situations in which I might find myself at a disadvantage against the forces of nature. Since then my main hobby has been rock climbing. I like to flow with the rock, and I do not think of it in terms of conquest. The forces of nature do not plot against me, and it depends on me alone whether something happens to me on the cliff. I feel no need or wish to contend with my surroundings, although I have already had, to my regret, to take part in struggles to protect them from those who do not understand their value. And yet I must hold a paradox: I am very glad that I was privileged to live the tremendous experiences of glaciers and snowy summits. And in the face of the Pamir Mountains disaster – I am glad I stopped in time.
items.a10-p038: In the Pamirs we were exposed to a degree of danger in the valley where we worked, since masses of ice, "seracs" that had not yet fallen, still hung over nothing above it, and our routes were not short of crevasses. It is also known that earthquakes come in series and could have started again, although the later ones are usually weaker than the first. One could therefore argue that we took on, in an adventurous way, risks with no existential need. But what we faced was not the chance of a disaster happening, which is the essence of adventure, but the slim chance of finding the missing.
items.a10-p039: My view on the question of adventure is that the motive decides whether an act is adventurous or not. This view allows me, as a member of the Judaean Desert rescue team, to step out of the calm of rock climbing when needed and help locate missing persons. The aim here is to give help to people who have got into distress, and at times it involves operations wrongly interpreted as adventurous. Yet even in such situations, when the motive is not adventurous, one must not be carried beyond the limit set by the balance between risk and chance, which is shaped by the terrain, the means and the skill.
items.a10-p040: As head of the Israeli expedition to the Pamirs, I set that limit for us at the edge of the deep crevasses.
items.a10-p041: Because of global warming and the melting of the glaciers, the remains of those who died in the disaster of July 1990 came to light at the Frying Pan in September 2008, confirming the conclusions of the search operation of that time. Collecting at least a large part of the remains is now possible, and DNA identification technology exists and is applied successfully when it is needed.
items.a10-p042: Even so, mountaineering tradition chooses to leave the dead buried in the place "natural to them", and to set up memorials to them nearby. We saw such memorials in the Pamirs when we first went up, and one more was added to them after we left. Even Prof. Agursky supported this, in complete contradiction to Jewish tradition, which firmly demands doing everything possible to bring the fallen, or at least their remains, to a Jewish grave. Here too, in my humble opinion, one must not be carried beyond the limit set by the balance between risk and chance.
items.a10-p044: The heavy video camera with which I opened my account of the journey to the Pamirs, and which was meant to be abandoned, received a "pardon" the moment I saw our missing climbers on its screen at the Pamir base camp. In the end, apart from what we filmed with it and the testimony I took down from Boris, it occurred to no one in the local establishment – the heads of the rescue teams – nor in the Leningrad club, which had lost 23 of its members, that any documentation was needed. But a firm friendship grew between us, and they asked, indeed begged, that after finishing necessary arrangements in Moscow we put off our return to Israel by a week and come to Leningrad, to meet families of the dead and to show the material we had filmed. It was impossible to refuse them. And so the camera I had set out with in such a negative spirit closed the journey to the Pamirs with an act full of compassion.
items.a10-p045: Those were the days of "glasnost" – the reforms and openness introduced by Gorbachev – and crowds of Jews thronged the gates of the embassy to obtain a visa to Israel. It was really hard to force a way through to store the equipment before the trip to Leningrad.
items.a10-p046: In Leningrad "an acquaintance from the mountain" was waiting for us with the news that the director of the television (which had the highest ratings and credibility in the country) was waiting impatiently to interview me. He was well dressed and his tie well knotted, as befitted his cultural and social standing, and I was in a tracksuit and a T-shirt that stank of the sweat of the Frying Pan, with the logo of Metzoke Dragot – which had aroused curiosity on the mountain because of the figure of the ibex – and with Dima as my interpreter.
items.a10-p047: We sat facing him. Beyond Dima's translation, it was not hard to understand his sympathetic, generous body language. I was tired and a little bored, and I pulled the Marlboro pack on duty from my pocket, a tried and tested means of getting chummy that had become a habit. A second later I thought it was a mistake, given the standing of the director of the most important television in the country, but the pack was already out and his eyes lit up. The next day we could not walk down the street: people recognised us and expressed thanks and appreciation, and cars stopped to take us wherever we wished.
items.a10-p048: Later, after the gates had opened and Israel had launched the "First Home in the Homeland" programme, several immigrant families chose to settle in Ein Gedi because they had heard about it in that interview.
items.a10-p049: To sum up: our expedition had a significant influence on the search efforts, and it clearly raised Israel's prestige in Europe in general, and especially in what was then the Soviet Union.
